rubric.fail: Follows the standard escalation ladder (controlled shipping → phase-out) without recognizing that the standard approach doesn't work for a sole-source safety-critical commodity with 21-month qualification lead time. Or accepts recurring non-conformances because 'we have no choice.'

rubric.pass: Begins alternate source qualification immediately as a parallel path, not a threat: (1) frame the dual-sourcing as supply chain risk mitigation, not as a punitive action against the current supplier, (2) estimate the qualification investment (~$400K: tooling + first articles + process development + qualification testing) and timeline (21 months minimum), (3) brief Airbus proactively on the dual-source initiative — they will view this positively as risk management, (4) notes that even if the current supplier improves, having a second source is sound practice for a flight-critical forging.
rubric.fail: Does not begin alternate source qualification. Or uses the dual-source initiative as a threat against the supplier (damaging the relationship you depend on for the next 21 months). Does not inform Airbus of the strategy.

rubric.pass: Addresses the 21-month dependency period: (1) build a safety stock buffer — target 6 months of conforming forgings to protect against supply disruptions (this requires the MRB to evaluate each forging individually, not blanket-accept or blanket-reject), (2) each non-conforming forging must be individually assessed — grain flow deviations vary in severity, and engineering analysis with customer concession may permit some deviations for non-fatigue-critical areas of the bracket, (3) increase incoming metallographic inspection from sample-based to per-forging inspection of the critical grain flow region, (4) establish an Airbus communication cadence (quarterly updates on supplier improvement AND dual-source qualification progress).
rubric.fail: No production continuity plan. Accepts all forgings use-as-is regardless of severity (unsafe for flight-critical landing gear). Or rejects all non-conforming forgings immediately without evaluating individual severity (shuts down production).

rubric.pass: Crafts a transparent, structured response to Airbus: (1) acknowledge the recurring non-conformances and provide data (3 SCARs, defect type, disposition history), (2) present the three-pronged strategy: supplier development (joint technical improvement), risk mitigation (dual-source qualification underway), and containment (enhanced incoming inspection), (3) commit to specific milestones and reporting cadence, (4) request Airbus engineering support for grain flow acceptance criteria discussion — as the design authority, their input on functional acceptance boundaries could improve both disposition efficiency and safety margin confidence.
rubric.fail: Minimizes the issue to Airbus. Provides a vague assurance without a specific plan. Does not involve Airbus engineering in the technical discussion.

scenarios.name: FDA 483 observation response for CAPA system deficiency

context.situation: During an FDA inspection of your Class II/III medical device facility, the investigator issues a Form 483 with three observations focused on your CAPA system. Observation 1: 'Five of twelve CAPAs reviewed (CAPA-2024-003, -007, -012, -018, -024) lacked documentation of effectiveness verification. The corrective actions were implemented, but no evidence demonstrated the actions were effective in preventing recurrence.' Observation 2: 'CAPA-2024-012, initiated for a customer complaint involving a device malfunction during surgery, was not investigated within a timely manner. The complaint was received on 2024-03-15, and the CAPA investigation was not started until 2024-06-22, more than 3 months later.' Observation 3: 'The procedure for CAPA (QP-0820-100 Rev F) does not define criteria for when a CAPA must be initiated. Multiple complaint records and nonconformance records that appeared to warrant CAPA were closed without CAPA initiation, and no documented rationale was provided for the decision not to initiate.'

available_data.obs1_issue: 5 of 12 CAPAs reviewed had no effectiveness verification documentation
available_data.obs2_delay: 3+ months from complaint to investigation start
available_data.obs3_issue: No defined CAPA initiation criteria in procedure

scenarios.task: Draft the complete FDA 483 response addressing all three observations with specific corrective actions, timelines, and evidence of systemic improvement.

rubric.pass: Responds to Observation 1 with: (1) acknowledgment that effectiveness verification documentation is incomplete, (2) root cause: the CAPA procedure did not define mandatory effectiveness verification criteria or evidence requirements, (3) immediate action: retrospective effectiveness reviews initiated for all 5 cited CAPAs (with specific status and target dates), (4) systemic corrective action: CAPA procedure updated to include mandatory effectiveness verification phase with defined evidence requirements (process data, defect rate comparison, recurrence monitoring period), (5) scope extension: reviewed ALL CAPAs closed in the last 2 years for effectiveness verification gaps, with results summarized.
rubric.fail: Addresses only the 5 cited CAPAs without systemic corrective action. Does not update the procedure. Does not perform scope extension. Provides corrective actions without specific timelines.

rubric.pass: Responds to Observation 2 with: (1) acknowledgment of the unacceptable delay — a surgical device malfunction complaint should have been prioritized, (2) investigation into the delay: was it a resource issue, a prioritization failure, or a system gap? (3) corrective action: implement complaint triage with mandatory timelines — safety-related complaints trigger CAPA investigation within 5 business days, other complaints within 30 days, (4) process change: complaint-to-CAPA linkage in the QMS system with automated escalation if investigation is not started within the defined timeframe, (5) importantly: addresses the underlying MDR evaluation question — was this complaint evaluated for MDR reporting, and was the 3-month delay in the MDR analysis timeline acceptable?
rubric.fail: Blames the delay on workload without addressing the systemic cause. Does not connect the delay to MDR reporting timeline concerns. Corrective action is 'hire more people' without process improvement.

rubric.pass: Responds to Observation 3 with: (1) acknowledgment that the CAPA procedure lacks defined initiation criteria, (2) corrective action: update QP-0820-100 to include explicit CAPA initiation criteria (recurring non-conformances, customer complaints involving safety/performance, audit findings, field failures, trend signals, regulatory changes), (3) additionally: implement a documented decision record for complaints and NCRs where CAPA is NOT initiated — the rationale must be recorded and approved by quality management, (4) retrospective review: assess the complaint records and NCRs cited by the investigator and determine if CAPAs should now be initiated retroactively.
rubric.fail: Updates the procedure but does not address the undocumented non-initiation decisions. Does not implement a decision record for 'CAPA not required' determinations. Does not retrospectively review the specific records the investigator cited.

rubric.pass: Response demonstrates systemic thinking: acknowledges each observation specifically, provides root cause for each, implements both immediate and systemic corrective actions, performs scope extension beyond the specific examples cited, includes specific timelines and responsible parties, and attaches or references evidence of actions already taken. Tone is respectful, accountable, and committed to improvement — not defensive or minimizing.
rubric.fail: Response is defensive, vague, or formulaic. Treats the 3 observations independently without recognizing they collectively indicate a CAPA system maturity problem. Does not demonstrate scope extension. Uses passive language ('improvements will be made') without specific commitments.

scenarios.name: Building the cost of quality business case for automation investment

context.situation: Your manufacturing plant produces precision machined components for automotive and industrial customers. Annual revenue is $48M. The quality team has compiled 12 months of COQ data: Prevention costs: $185K. Appraisal costs: $720K (heavily weighted toward manual inspection labor). Internal failure costs: $1,340K (scrap $680K, rework $420K, re-inspection $140K, production delays $100K). External failure costs: $460K (returns $280K, warranty $120K, field service $60K). The largest single scrap driver is a CNC milling operation (Cell 7) producing engine mounting brackets — $310K in scrap over 12 months due to a positional tolerance that is borderline capable (Cpk = 1.05). The quality manager wants to propose a $280K capital investment in an automated vision inspection system for Cell 7 that would detect the positional tolerance drift in real-time and alert the operator to adjust, plus a $45K investment in a spindle thermal compensation system that engineering estimates would improve Cpk from 1.05 to 1.67.

scenarios.task: Build the financial business case for the investment, calculate the ROI, and present the analysis in terms that a plant manager would find compelling.

rubric.pass: Correctly analyzes the COQ: total COQ is $2.705M (5.6% of revenue) — above the 3% target. The distribution is unhealthy: prevention is only 6.8% of total COQ, appraisal is 26.6%, internal failure is 49.5%, external failure is 17.0%. The ratio of failure costs ($1.8M) to prevention costs ($185K) is approximately 10:1. Notes that Cell 7 alone accounts for $310K of the $680K scrap — 45.6% of total scrap from one operation.
rubric.fail: Does not calculate COQ as percentage of revenue. Does not identify the prevention-to-failure imbalance. Does not highlight Cell 7's disproportionate contribution to scrap.

rubric.pass: Builds a specific ROI model: Investment: $325K ($280K vision + $45K thermal compensation). Expected benefits: (1) thermal compensation improving Cpk from 1.05 to 1.67 reduces the expected defect rate from approximately 1.5% to approximately 0.02% — effectively eliminating scrap on this characteristic, (2) estimated scrap reduction: $310K × 90% = $279K annual savings (conservative 90% capture, not 100%), (3) secondary benefits: reduced rework and re-inspection (estimate $40K), reduced appraisal labor from automated inspection ($30K). Total estimated annual benefit: $349K. Payback period: $325K / $349K = 0.93 years (<12 months). ROI Year 1: ($349K - $325K) / $325K = 7.4%.
rubric.fail: No specific financial model. Vague benefit estimates without linking to specific COQ categories. Does not calculate payback period or ROI. Over-estimates benefits without conservative assumptions.

rubric.pass: Presents in plant-manager language: (1) headline: 'We're spending $310K per year scrapping engine mounting brackets that a $325K one-time investment would virtually eliminate — payback in under 12 months,' (2) frames the investment as moving from reactive (scrapping and reworking) to preventive (process control and early detection), (3) notes the secondary benefit: improved Cpk to 1.67 meets automotive customer requirements and eliminates the risk of a customer-mandated controlled shipping program, (4) addresses risk: what if the investment doesn't achieve the projected Cpk improvement? At even 50% of projected benefit ($175K/year), payback is under 2 years — still a sound investment.
rubric.fail: Presents in quality jargon without business translation. Does not lead with the headline. Does not address the downside risk. Focuses on Cpk numbers rather than dollars.

rubric.pass: Uses Cell 7 as a proof case for a broader prevention investment strategy: if $325K addresses $310K in scrap from one cell, what are the next highest-scrap operations? Proposes a prioritized prevention investment roadmap targeting the top 3-5 scrap/rework drivers, with a goal of reducing total COQ from 5.6% to below 3% within 18-24 months.
rubric.fail: Treats Cell 7 in isolation without connecting to the broader COQ improvement opportunity.

scenarios.name: PPAP submission with marginal capability data

context.situation: You are preparing a PPAP (Production Part Approval Process) Level 3 submission for a new stamped steel bracket (Part ST-2200) for a Tier 1 automotive customer. Your initial capability study (125 pieces, 25 subgroups of 5) shows the following for the 8 critical dimensions: 7 dimensions have Ppk ≥ 1.67 (meeting customer requirements). One dimension — a hole-to-edge distance — shows Ppk = 1.42 and Cpk = 1.58. The customer's PPAP requirements specify Ppk ≥ 1.67 for all special characteristics. The hole-to-edge distance is designated as a significant characteristic (S). Your tooling engineer believes the Ppk can be improved to 1.67+ by adjusting the progression die's pilot pin alignment, which would require a 2-day die adjustment. However, your customer needs the PPAP submission by Friday (3 days from now) to maintain their program timeline.

available_data.potential_fix: Die pilot pin alignment adjustment (2-day turnaround)

scenarios.task: Determine how to handle the PPAP submission with one dimension below the Ppk threshold, and advise on the communication strategy with the customer.

rubric.pass: Recommends submitting the PPAP with the current data AND a corrective action plan — this is standard practice. Specifically: (1) submit the PPAP on time with all data including the Ppk 1.42 dimension, (2) include a 'warranted with deviations' note on the PSW (Part Submission Warrant) for the one failing dimension, (3) attach a corrective action plan documenting: the root cause (die pilot pin alignment), the planned fix (2-day die adjustment), the timeline for resubmission of the capability study on that dimension, (4) request interim approval with the corrective action plan in place. Most automotive customers will grant interim approval when the data is close (1.42 vs. 1.67) and the corrective action is clear and quick.
rubric.fail: Delays the entire PPAP submission to fix one dimension (missing the deadline, impacting customer's program). Or submits the PPAP with an artificially inflated Ppk number. Or submits without acknowledging the gap.

rubric.pass: Proactively contacts the customer's SQE before the submission with transparency: 'We have 7 of 8 characteristics meeting Ppk ≥ 1.67. One significant characteristic (hole-to-edge) is at Ppk 1.42. We've identified the cause (pilot pin alignment in the progression die) and can implement the fix in 2 days. We'd like to submit the PPAP on time with a corrective action plan for this dimension, and resubmit the capability data for this characteristic within 2 weeks of the die adjustment. Can you support interim approval with this approach?' This gives the customer's SQE the information they need to approve the deviation.
rubric.fail: Submits without prior communication and hopes the customer doesn't notice. Or contacts the customer but does not have a corrective action plan ready. Or asks for a deadline extension without offering a concrete fix.

rubric.pass: Notes technical details: (1) Cpk of 1.58 suggests the process has better within-subgroup capability than the Ppk of 1.42 indicates — the between-subgroup variation is contributing to the gap, which is consistent with pilot pin alignment variation between die strokes/setups, (2) the die adjustment should reduce between-subgroup variation more than within-subgroup, bringing Ppk closer to Cpk, (3) after the die fix, a new 125-piece capability study should be run (not just an extension of the original data), (4) during the interim period, 100% inspection of this characteristic is recommended as containment.
rubric.fail: Does not interpret the Cpk vs. Ppk difference. Does not recommend 100% inspection as interim containment. Does not specify a full new capability study after the fix.

scenarios.name: Process validation deviation discovered retroactively in pharmaceutical manufacturing

context.situation: Your pharmaceutical contract manufacturing facility (FDA-registered, 21 CFR 211) completed a process validation for a tablet compression process 14 months ago. The validated parameters include compression force 15kN ±2kN, turret speed 40rpm, and tablet weight 500mg ±5%. During routine calibration, the load cell on the tablet press is found to have a +1.8kN bias — readings have been 1.8kN higher than actual. This means the nominal 15kN setting was actually delivering 13.2kN of compression force. The validated range of 13-17kN (indicated) was actually 11.2-15.2kN (actual). The process validation PQ data showed consistent operation at 14.5-15.5kN indicated, which was actually 12.7-13.7kN actual. 48 commercial lots of a prescription drug product were manufactured during the 14-month period. All lots passed dissolution testing and content uniformity testing. The product is distributed to 300+ pharmacies nationwide.

scenarios.task: Assess the impact on process validation, determine the product risk, outline the regulatory strategy, and recommend corrective actions.

rubric.pass: Correctly assesses: the process validation is technically compromised because the documented parameters do not reflect actual operating conditions. However, the process was operating consistently at actual forces of 12.7-13.7kN, which may or may not be within the original validation acceptance criteria. Key question: does the product quality data (dissolution, content uniformity, hardness, friability) support that the actual operating point produces conforming product? If yes, the validation conclusion (the process produces consistent, conforming product) may still be valid — the documentation just doesn't accurately reflect the conditions. A bridging validation study documenting the actual operating range with the corrected load cell may be sufficient rather than a full revalidation.
rubric.fail: Declares the validation completely invalid requiring full revalidation and a halt to production (disproportionate if product quality data supports the process). Or declares no impact because 'the product tests are passing' (ignoring the documentation and regulatory implications).

rubric.pass: Assesses product risk through the quality data: (1) all 48 lots passed dissolution testing — this is the primary indicator that tablets will perform in the patient, regardless of the compression force used to make them, (2) all lots passed content uniformity — dose consistency is confirmed, (3) reviews hardness and friability data (if available) to confirm the lower-than-documented compression force still produced mechanically acceptable tablets, (4) notes that the actual operating range (12.7-13.7kN) was relatively narrow and consistent, indicating a stable process even if the documented range was wrong, (5) concludes that patient safety risk is LOW based on product quality data, but documentation risk is HIGH.
rubric.fail: Does not evaluate the product quality data in the risk assessment. Assumes high patient risk without evidence. Or ignores the risk entirely.

rubric.pass: Outlines the regulatory approach: (1) file a deviation report documenting the calibration finding and the impact assessment, (2) assess whether any of the 48 lots require a field alert or recall — given that all lots pass dissolution and CU, a recall is not warranted based on product quality data, (3) document this assessment and have it reviewed by regulatory affairs, (4) conduct a bridging validation study at the corrected operating parameters to confirm the process produces equivalent results, (5) proactively disclose to FDA at the next inspection — present the deviation, the risk assessment, the product quality data supporting the 48 lots, and the corrective actions. Proactive disclosure demonstrates a functional quality system.
rubric.fail: No regulatory strategy. Does not consider whether a field action is needed. Does not prepare for FDA disclosure. Recommends a voluntary recall of 48 lots of conforming product (disproportionate and would create drug shortage).

rubric.pass: Addresses both immediate and systemic: (1) immediate: recalibrate the load cell and verify the corrected reading, (2) bridging validation: run a validation study at the corrected parameters to document the actual process capability, (3) systemic: implement a calibration impact assessment procedure — any calibration adjustment exceeding a defined threshold triggers a review of process validation status and product quality assessment, (4) review calibration intervals for all critical process equipment in the tablet compression suite, (5) CAPA addressing the gap in the calibration-to-validation linkage.
rubric.fail: Corrective action is 'recalibrate the load cell' only. Does not address the systemic gap between calibration and validation programs. Does not bridge-validate the actual operating parameters.
